summary: For ages 5–7, help children KNOW and feel a few vivid, true stories of polar explorers: Amundsen reaching the South Pole first, Scott reaching it but dying on the return, and Shackleton losing his ship Endurance yet bringing all of the Endurance crew home. Teach it as narrative with a beginning, danger and ending, anchoring the hardship in things a young child can feel (bitter cold, hunger, darkness, being far from home) and surfacing the reframe that 'brave' and 'successful' are not the same thing. This fits the UK KS1 History aim of teaching the lives of significant individuals in the past (explorers), alongside a cold-environments science context.
misconceptions: Being brave means always winning — Scott and Shackleton are heroes despite not achieving their goals
Explorers went alone — these were teams who depended on each other
It happened long, long ago in a made-up way — these are real people from about 100 years ago with real photographs
They could just call for help — there were no phones, planes or rescue; they had to save themselves
Reaching the Pole was the only thing that mattered — getting the team home mattered just as much

activities.title: Three explorers, three stories (illustrated narrative with reveals)
steps: Look at a wide wintry picture of the ship Endurance trapped in white pack ice under a low sun.

Reveal the story in order: Endurance is crushed and sinks; the crew camps on the ice and reaches Elephant Island in boats; Shackleton and a small party sail through rough seas to South Georgia to seek help; a rescue ship later returns for the men left behind.
Reveal Shackleton's outcome: 'He brought all the men of the Endurance crew home — not one was lost.'

For Scott, Amundsen and Shackleton, ask whether they reached the South Pole: Amundsen reached it first; Scott reached it but died on the return; Shackleton did not reach it on the Endurance expedition, but all members of the Endurance party survived.
(Optional) Reveal a 'what they packed' picture — dogs, sledges, tents and warm clothing such as furs and wool — to show how the explorers tried to survive the cold.
Talk about a time you kept going when something was really hard, and connect it to the explorers' endurance.
activities.insight: These were real people from more than 100 years ago who faced real danger as a team; being brave is not the same as winning — Shackleton never reached his goal but kept every member of the Endurance crew alive.

activities.title: Talking with Shackleton (spoken role-play extension)
steps: Pretend to talk with a warm, friendly Shackleton and ask how he kept his men going when the ship was lost.
Ask him what the hardest and coldest moments were, and how the team helped each other.
Say back in your own words one thing Shackleton did to bring everyone home.
activities.insight: Leadership and care for the team — not reaching the goal — are what make Shackleton remembered as brave.

activities.title: Who did what? (sorting to firm up recall)
steps: Sort three portrait cards — Amundsen, Scott, Shackleton — each with one memorable fact.
Match each explorer to his story: Amundsen (first to the Pole), Scott (reached it, died returning), Shackleton (ship crushed, saved all of the Endurance crew).
Name at least one thing that made polar exploration hard: freezing cold, running short of food, or thick ice.
Say in one sentence why Shackleton is remembered as brave even though he never reached his goal.
activities.insight: Children can keep the three stories distinct and tie each explorer to his outcome, while still holding onto the point that getting the team home mattered as much as reaching the Pole.

checkQuestion: Long ago, brave explorers tried to reach the South Pole. Amundsen from Norway got there first; Scott from Britain arrived later and sadly died on the way back; and Shackleton's ship the Endurance got crushed by the ice. A friend says 'Amundsen only won because he got lucky, and Shackleton's trip was a total disaster.' Do you think it was just luck — and was Shackleton's story only a disaster, or is there something amazing in it?
checkAnswer: It wasn't just luck: Amundsen won because he PLANNED carefully — using dog sleds and preparing well — while Scott's journey was far harder and he tragically died returning. And Shackleton's story, although his ship was crushed, is famous as amazing because he got EVERY one of his men home ALIVE through an incredible rescue journey. So it's a story of courage, planning and endurance, not just luck or disaster.
